subtopic_detail: Preoperative biochemical correction before pyloromyotomy in an infant with hypochloraemic alkalosis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 5 week old boy whose ultrasound has just been reported. His mother says he brings the whole feed back forcefully, sometimes clearing the edge of the change table, and then wants to feed again straight away.

He has lost 200 g since his two week check and his nappies have been drier than usual for three days. He is alert with a sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. The surgical registrar telephones to say a theatre slot is free this evening and asks whether to take him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 172/min, blood pressure 74/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Ultrasound: Pyloric muscle thickness 4.6 mm, channel length 19 mm
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfer to theatre now because the obstruction needs urgent surgical relief
options.rationale: The obstruction is mechanical but not strangulating, so there is no ischaemic emergency and nothing is gained by operating on an alkalotic infant. Anaesthesia in uncorrected metabolic alkalosis carries a recognised risk of postoperative apnoea. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Give a bolus of five per cent dextrose and book theatre for this evening
options.rationale: Dextrose without sodium and chloride does not replace the losses that generated the alkalosis and risks worsening the hyponatraemia. Correction requires chloride specifically, which this fluid lacks. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Rehydrate with sodium chloride and added potassium until the biochemistry corrects
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting of gastric contents strips hydrogen and chloride, producing a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that the kidney sustains until chloride is replaced. Pyloromyotomy is an elective procedure performed only once the chloride and bicarbonate have normalised, because uncorrected alkalosis depresses the central respiratory drive under anaesthesia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Pass a nasogastric tube and start intravenous antibiotics before theatre
options.rationale: There is no infective process here, and continuous nasogastric drainage removes yet more gastric chloride and worsens the alkalosis. Free drainage is used for a distal obstruction with bilious aspirates, which is a different clinical problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

options.text: Start oral rehydration solution and recheck the electrolytes in twelve hours
options.rationale: Oral fluid will not be retained past a mechanically obstructed pylorus, so the deficit persists while the delay accumulates. Oral rehydration is the route of choice in gastroenteritis, where the gut remains patent. (Source: RCH CPG: Pyloric stenosis)

explanation.summary: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents in the third to sixth week with non bilious forceful vomiting in a baby who remains hungry, and the diagnosis is confirmed on ultrasound by muscle thickness above about 3 mm with a channel longer than 15 mm. The metabolic consequence is the part that kills: loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, which the kidney perpetuates by exchanging hydrogen for sodium once chloride is unavailable, generating the paradoxical aciduria. Pyloromyotomy is therefore never an emergency, and operating before correction exposes the infant to postoperative apnoea from a centrally depressed respiratory drive. Resuscitation with sodium chloride and potassium typically takes 24 to 48 hours, and surgery follows once the chloride exceeds about 100 mmol/L and the bicarbonate has fallen below about 30 mmol/L.
key_points: The vomiting is non bilious and the infant remains hungry afterwards
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria is the signature
Pyloromyotomy is elective and follows biochemical correction
Chloride replacement is what allows the kidney to excrete bicarbonate
Uncorrected alkalosis predisposes to postoperative apnoea
explanation.pearls: Aim for a chloride above 100 mmol/L and a bicarbonate below 30 mmol/L before pyloromyotomy, which usually takes 24 to 48 hours of sodium chloride with added potassium once the infant is passing urine.

subtopic_detail: Choosing urate lowering prophylaxis for tumour lysis risk when glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency is known
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 6 year old boy with newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. He is alert and well perfused, and induction chemotherapy is planned to start tomorrow morning.

His presenting blood film and counts show a heavy circulating blast burden, and his biochemistry already shows a raised urate before any treatment. He was investigated for prolonged jaundice as a newborn and was found then to have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, confirmed on enzyme assay after the jaundice settled. The haematology consultant asks you to write up his tumour lysis prophylaxis.

data_table.Full blood count: White cell count 184 x10^9/L with 88 per cent blasts, haemoglobin 76 g/L (115-135), platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Biochemistry: Urate 0.58 mmol/L (0.12-0.32), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), phosphate 1.9 mmol/L (1.0-1.8), creatinine 74 micromol/L (30-60)
data_table.Past history: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency confirmed on enzyme assay in infancy

lead_in: Which prophylactic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Give rasburicase now because the urate and white cell count are both high
options.rationale: The risk profile does argue for aggressive urate control, but rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide as it degrades urate and precipitates severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in enzyme deficient patients. His deficiency makes this an absolute contraindication rather than a relative one. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Give rasburicase at half the usual dose with close monitoring of haemoglobin
options.rationale: The haemolytic reaction is not dose dependent in a way that makes reduction safe, and monitoring detects the injury rather than preventing it. Dose reduction is a strategy for renal clearance issues, not for an enzymatic contraindication. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Withhold urate lowering therapy and rely on intravenous hydration alone
options.rationale: Hydration is the backbone of prophylaxis but is insufficient by itself when the urate is already elevated with this blast burden. Hydration alone suits a low risk tumour with a normal baseline urate. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Start urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and give rasburicase
options.rationale: Alkalinisation is no longer recommended because it promotes calcium phosphate deposition in the tubules while the patient is already hyperphosphataemic, and it is redundant alongside effective urate lowering. The rasburicase component remains contraindicated regardless. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

options.text: Start allopurinol with generous intravenous hydration and monitor the urate
options.rationale: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase and prevents further urate formation without any oxidative stress on red cells, making it the safe choice when rasburicase cannot be used. Combined with high volume intravenous hydration it protects renal function while the blast burden falls, accepting that existing urate is cleared more slowly than with the enzyme. (Source: eviQ: Tumour lysis syndrome)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome follows the rapid breakdown of a large tumour burden, releasing potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids that are metabolised to urate, with acute kidney injury the feared endpoint. Risk stratification in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia rests on the white cell count, the baseline urate and renal function, and this child is high risk on all three. Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase that converts existing urate to the far more soluble allantoin and is the agent of choice for high risk disease, but the reaction liberates hydrogen peroxide, which red cells lacking glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase cannot detoxify. The result is brisk haemolysis with methaemoglobinaemia, so the enzyme deficiency converts the preferred drug into a contraindicated one and allopurinol with aggressive hydration becomes the fallback.
key_points: High white cell count, raised baseline urate and renal impairment define high risk
Rasburicase degrades existing urate; allopurinol only prevents new formation
Rasburicase is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended and worsens phosphate deposition
Hydration underpins every regimen regardless of the agent chosen
explanation.pearls: Screen for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency before rasburicase in any patient of African, Mediterranean or Southeast Asian ancestry, because the resulting haemolysis with methaemoglobinaemia does not respond to methylene blue in these patients.

subtopic_detail: Deciding on prophylactic fixation of the unaffected hip when a slip occurs with an underlying endocrinopathy
stem:
You are the registrar in the orthopaedic clinic seeing an 11 year old boy referred with three weeks of left knee ache and a limp that his mother says has slowly worsened. There was no injury.

He was diagnosed with hypothyroidism two years ago and takes thyroxine, though his mother admits doses are often missed. On examination the left leg lies in slight external rotation and the hip rolls outwards as you flex it. Plain films of both hips are reviewed with the consultant, who confirms a mild stable slip on the left and asks you to consent the family for surgery.

data_table.Examination: Left leg externally rotated, obligate external rotation on hip flexion, able to weight bear with a limp
data_table.Growth: Weight above the 97th centile, height on the 25th centile
data_table.Imaging: Mild stable slip of the left capital femoral epiphysis, right epiphysis not displaced with an open physis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative plan?

options.text: Pin the affected hip alone and review the other hip clinically each year
options.rationale: Clinical surveillance alone is the default for an otherwise healthy adolescent with a unilateral slip, where the contralateral risk is roughly one in five and presentation is usually symptomatic. It underprotects a child whose endocrinopathy raises that risk substantially. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Pin the affected hip and pin the opposite hip during the same anaesthetic
options.rationale: An underlying endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism raises the rate of a subsequent contralateral slip towards and beyond half, which is the accepted threshold for prophylactic fixation. Doing both hips under one anaesthetic avoids a second operation and prevents a slip that could present late with avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Pin the affected hip and arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the other hip
options.rationale: Imaging the asymptomatic side can identify a pre slip but does not alter the decision in a child who already meets the criteria for prophylactic fixation on endocrine grounds. It adds cost and a further anaesthetic in a young child without changing the plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Attempt closed reduction of the slip before any internal fixation is done
options.rationale: Forceful reduction of a stable slip disrupts the retinacular vessels and is the principal iatrogenic cause of avascular necrosis in this condition. Fixation is performed in situ, accepting the existing deformity. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

options.text: Treat in traction without weight bearing and delay any operative fixation
options.rationale: Non operative management allows progression of the slip and does not stabilise the physis, so it is not used for a diagnosed slip. Traction has no role once the diagnosis is radiologically confirmed. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

explanation.summary: A slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and classically presents with knee or thigh pain rather than hip pain, which is why a limping adolescent needs the hip examined and imaged regardless of where the pain is felt. Treatment is in situ screw fixation, since attempting to reduce the slip strips the posterior retinacular blood supply and causes avascular necrosis. The contested decision is the opposite hip: baseline contralateral slip rates sit near 20 per cent and most units accept clinical follow up, but prophylactic fixation becomes the recommended course when the risk is markedly elevated. The recognised high risk groups are children with endocrinopathy such as hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency or renal osteodystrophy, and those presenting at a young chronological age relative to their skeletal maturity.
key_points: Knee or thigh pain with a limp requires hip imaging in an adolescent
Fixation is performed in situ because reduction risks avascular necrosis
Contralateral slip occurs in about one in five otherwise healthy children
Endocrinopathy or young age at presentation justifies prophylactic fixation
Obligate external rotation on hip flexion is the classic examination finding
explanation.pearls: Suspect an underlying endocrinopathy when a slip occurs below ten years of age or in a child whose height is well below the weight centile, and check thyroid function before discharge.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric hip conditions

subtopic_detail: Antiviral decision for a symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection confirmed within the first three weeks
stem:
You are the registrar reviewing a 12 day old girl on the postnatal ward whose newborn hearing screen failed on both sides and was not passed on repeat.

She was born at term but was small, and the midwives noted a scattered rash of pinpoint red spots on her trunk that does not blanch. Her head circumference sits well below her weight centile. A urine sample collected on day 10 has returned positive for cytomegalovirus on nucleic acid testing, and her cranial ultrasound shows scattered calcification. Her mother recalls a flu like illness in the second trimester.

data_table.Growth: Birthweight below the 3rd centile, head circumference below the 3rd centile
data_table.Examination: Non blanching petechial rash over the trunk, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Urine cytomegalovirus nucleic acid test positive on day 10, alanine aminotransferase 180 U/L (less than 45), platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400), cranial ultrasound shows periventricular calcification
data_table.Hearing: Automated auditory brainstem response failed bilaterally on initial and repeat screening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe with audiology follow up alone because antiviral therapy has no benefit
options.rationale: Observation is the correct course for asymptomatic infection detected incidentally, where treatment has not been shown to help and carries toxicity. This baby has multisystem disease, which is precisely the group in whom treatment improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Give intravenous ganciclovir for six weeks and then stop all antiviral therapy
options.rationale: Six weeks of intravenous ganciclovir was the older regimen and is now used only for the initial phase when oral therapy is not tolerated, because six months of oral treatment produces better hearing and developmental outcomes. Stopping at six weeks forfeits that additional benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Start oral valganciclovir only if the hearing loss progresses over the first year
options.rationale: The treatment benefit depends on starting within the first month of life, so deferring until progression is documented moves therapy outside the window in which it works. Later deterioration is managed with amplification and implantation rather than with antivirals. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Start oral valganciclovir now and continue it for six months with monitoring
options.rationale: Symptomatic congenital infection confirmed within the first three weeks of life is treated with six months of oral valganciclovir begun before one month of age, which improves hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes compared with shorter or later therapy. Neutropenia is the dose limiting toxicity, so the full blood count is monitored weekly at first and then monthly. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

options.text: Give cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin as a single dose and monitor her hearing
options.rationale: Hyperimmune globulin has been studied mainly as an antenatal intervention to prevent transmission and has not shown benefit as postnatal treatment of established disease. It does not replace antiviral therapy in a symptomatic newborn. (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital cytomegalovirus)

explanation.summary: Congenital cytomegalovirus is the commonest congenital infection and the leading non genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, which is why a failed newborn hearing screen should prompt consideration of it. Diagnosis must be established on urine or saliva nucleic acid testing within the first three weeks of life, because a positive sample after that point cannot distinguish congenital infection from postnatal acquisition through breast milk or saliva. Treatment is reserved for symptomatic disease, defined by features such as growth restriction, microcephaly, petechiae, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification or sensorineural hearing loss. Six months of oral valganciclovir started within the first month improves both hearing and neurodevelopmental outcomes, while asymptomatic infants are followed with serial audiology rather than treated.
key_points: Confirmation requires urine or saliva testing within the first three weeks of life
Only symptomatic infants are treated with antivirals
Six months of oral valganciclovir beats six weeks of intravenous therapy
Therapy must begin within the first month to achieve benefit
Neutropenia is the dose limiting toxicity and requires scheduled counts
explanation.pearls: A positive cytomegalovirus test after 21 days of age cannot distinguish congenital from postnatally acquired infection, so retrieve the stored newborn screening card for testing if the diagnosis is raised later.
